title: Polytrauma & Hemorrhagic Shock: Primary Survey, Hemorrhage Control and Massive Transfusion
html:
Major trauma is managed by threats to life, not by the injury that looks most dramatic. Catastrophic external bleeding, airway obstruction, tension physiology, massive hemothorax, and internal hemorrhage can kill within minutes. The RN supports a structured primary survey, controls compressible bleeding, recognizes compensated shock, activates coordinated blood-based resuscitation, prevents hypothermia and hypocalcemia, and helps move the patient rapidly toward definitive hemorrhage control.

Learning goals

  • Apply an XABCDE trauma sequence while protecting the spine and preventing hypothermia.
  • Recognize hemorrhagic shock before hypotension and identify common concealed bleeding compartments.
  • Use direct pressure, wound packing, tourniquets, and pelvic stabilization safely.
  • Coordinate massive transfusion, warming, calcium and coagulation monitoring while limiting unnecessary crystalloid.
  • Differentiate resuscitation endpoints from temporary improvement and prioritize operative or interventional hemorrhage control.
  • Perform repeated primary and secondary surveys to detect deterioration and missed injuries.

Start with XABCDE and repeat it

X—exsanguinating external hemorrhage: Immediately control obvious catastrophic bleeding while the team activates trauma resources. A—airway with cervical-spine protection: Assess patency, voice, blood, vomit, facial injury, mental status, and the need for definitive airway control while maintaining indicated spinal motion restriction. B—breathing: Inspect, palpate, auscultate, and compare chest expansion, breath sounds, oxygenation, work of breathing, and hemodynamics. C—circulation: Assess pulses, pressure trend, skin, capillary refill, mentation, bleeding and likely internal sources. D—disability: Establish pupils, motor response, glucose and a reproducible neurologic baseline. E—exposure/environment: fully inspect while actively preventing hypothermia.

The sequence is not a one-time checklist. Reassess after airway intervention, chest decompression, blood administration, transport, imaging, procedures, and any deterioration. A new airway or breathing emergency interrupts the survey. In an actively exsanguinating patient, hemorrhage control and circulation support may proceed concurrently with airway maneuvers rather than waiting for a perfectly completed sequence.

Treat immediate breathing threats clinically

Tension pneumothorax can cause severe respiratory distress, unilateral reduced breath sounds, hypotension, distended neck veins when volume permits, tracheal deviation as a late sign, and obstructive shock. Massive hemothorax can cause reduced breath sounds with shock from blood loss. An open chest wound, flail segment, or airway disruption can rapidly impair ventilation. Activate the trauma pathway and prepare immediate protocol-directed decompression or chest drainage; an unstable patient should not wait for routine imaging to treat a clinical life threat.

After intervention, reassess breath sounds, chest movement, oxygenation, ventilation, pressure, pulse, mental status, drainage, insertion site and equipment. Persistent shock may reflect continued thoracic bleeding, abdominal or pelvic hemorrhage, tamponade, neurogenic shock, or more than one mechanism.

Normal blood pressure does not exclude hemorrhagic shock

Early blood loss may produce anxiety, tachypnea, cool skin, delayed capillary refill, narrowing pulse pressure, tachycardia, thirst, weakness, or subtle confusion while systolic pressure remains normal. Young adults can compensate until sudden collapse; older adults, athletes, pregnant patients, and people taking beta blockers may not show classic patterns. A falling trend and clinical trajectory are more important than one threshold.

Shock index—heart rate divided by systolic pressure—can support risk recognition, but it does not diagnose hemorrhage or replace assessment. Hemoglobin may initially remain near baseline because whole blood is lost before redistribution or fluids change the measured concentration. Lactate and base deficit help trend tissue stress but are influenced by other causes. Do not delay hemorrhage control for a low initial score or reassuring first laboratory result.

Search the floor and major internal compartments

Major blood loss may be external or concealed in the chest, abdomen, pelvis or retroperitoneum, and long bones or soft tissues. Inspect the back, axillae, perineum and scalp when safe; assess chest symmetry, abdomen, pelvis, long-bone deformity, expanding swelling, wounds, drains and the scene or mechanism. Anticoagulants, antiplatelets and bleeding disorders lower the threshold for concern.

Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma (FAST/eFAST) can identify selected pericardial, pleural and intraperitoneal fluid or pneumothorax, but a negative examination does not exclude early bleeding, hollow-viscus injury, retroperitoneal or pelvic hemorrhage. Hemodynamically unstable patients require a rapid trauma decision pathway; do not delay definitive treatment merely to complete every CT image.

Control compressible bleeding now

Use PPE and expose the source. Apply firm direct pressure with gauze or cloth and maintain it rather than repeatedly lifting the dressing to look. Pack an appropriate deep wound tightly to its source and maintain pressure when trained and the anatomy permits; do not blindly pack the chest or abdomen. Add a pressure dressing without making it a hidden tourniquet.

For life-threatening extremity bleeding not controlled promptly by pressure, apply an approved tourniquet according to training and device instructions, proximal to the wound and not over a joint. Tighten until bleeding stops and distal pulse is absent when assessable, secure it, document the exact time, keep it visible, and do not loosen it periodically. A second tourniquet may be required under protocol. Pain from an effective tourniquet is expected and is not a reason to release it while major bleeding continues.

Impaled objects are generally stabilized in place rather than removed outside a controlled surgical plan. If an object blocks lifesaving access or transport, the trauma team directs management. Never clamp a bleeding vessel blindly; protect pressure, perfusion, nerves and surrounding tissue.

Suspected pelvic hemorrhage needs early stabilization

A high-energy mechanism, pelvic pain or instability, leg-length or rotational change, perineal bruising, urethral blood, or unexplained shock may indicate pelvic-ring injury. Avoid repeatedly “springing” or rocking the pelvis; this can disrupt clots. Apply an approved pelvic binder or sheet at the level of the greater trochanters, not the waist or iliac crests, when indicated by the trauma pathway.

After application, verify position, pressure, skin, distal neurovascular status and ongoing shock. The binder is temporary hemorrhage control, not definitive treatment. Prolonged pressure can injure skin. Prepare for preperitoneal packing, angiographic embolization, operative stabilization or other local pathways while continuing to search for simultaneous chest or abdominal bleeding.

Damage-control resuscitation prioritizes blood and hemostasis

Establish rapid vascular access without delaying hemorrhage control. Obtain pretransfusion specimens when feasible, but life-threatening bleeding may require emergency-release blood. Activate the facility massive-transfusion protocol (MTP) early when the pattern predicts ongoing major blood need rather than ordering isolated units one at a time. Communicate activation, cooler receipt, component verification, administration, laboratory trends, source-control plan and explicit MTP termination.

Damage-control resuscitation limits unnecessary crystalloid, uses warmed whole blood or balanced red cells, plasma and platelets according to the local protocol, replaces fibrinogen when indicated, and moves rapidly to operative, endovascular or procedural control. Ratios are an initial system—not a permanent target for every patient. Transition to laboratory- or viscoelastic-guided therapy when the team and results permit.

Permissive hypotension may be selected before hemostasis to avoid dislodging clots and worsening dilution, but it is not suitable for every patient. Suspected traumatic brain injury, pregnancy, spinal-cord perfusion needs, older or chronically hypertensive patients and prolonged transport may require different goals. The RN follows the individualized trauma target and watches mentation, pulses, skin, urine and bleeding—not simply a “low” pressure number.

Prevent the lethal diamond

Hemorrhage and exposure promote hypothermia; poor perfusion produces acidosis; tissue injury, shock and dilution worsen coagulopathy; citrate in blood products contributes to hypocalcemia. These problems amplify bleeding and myocardial dysfunction. Warm the room, patient, IV fluids and blood with approved devices; minimize unnecessary exposure and wet linens; and monitor core temperature.

During MTP, trend ECG, ionized calcium, potassium, blood gas and acid-base status, lactate or base deficit, hemoglobin, platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, viscoelastic tests when used, urine, temperature, bleeding and perfusion. Administer protocol-directed calcium and other products safely. Citrate-related hypocalcemia can cause hypotension, weak contraction, prolonged QT and dysrhythmia. Do not inject calcium into the same line as incompatible blood products without the approved setup.

TXA and reversal are time- and patient-specific

Tranexamic acid (TXA) may be used early for selected trauma patients with significant bleeding or high hemorrhage risk under the local protocol. Benefit depends on early administration, generally within three hours of injury; it is not routine for every injured patient and should not delay blood or hemorrhage control. Verify injury time, indication, contraindications, dose and infusion method.

Identify anticoagulant or antiplatelet agent, last dose, kidney function and bleeding site immediately. Warfarin, dabigatran, factor Xa inhibitors and heparins require different reversal strategies; vitamin K does not reverse every drug. Draw indicated studies without delaying emergency drug-specific reversal and source control. Reassess for thrombosis as well as hemostasis.

Definitive control—not pressure normalization—is the goal

Blood products can restore oxygen carrying capacity and hemostatic components, but they do not repair a torn vessel or ruptured organ. A transient responder who improves and then deteriorates is still bleeding until proven otherwise. Prepare for damage-control surgery, interventional radiology, endoscopy, thoracic intervention or other source control based on anatomy, physiology and resources.

Report exact response: amount and type of product, pressure and pulse trend, mentation, skin, urine, temperature, calcium, acid-base status, visible bleeding and drain output. Vasopressors do not replace blood and hemorrhage control in hypovolemic shock; selected use belongs to the trauma team when physiology is mixed or perfusion remains inadequate.

Secondary survey begins only after immediate threats

After resuscitation is underway and life threats are addressed, obtain an AMPLE history—Allergies, Medications, Past illnesses or Pregnancy, Last meal, and Events/environment—and complete a systematic head-to-toe examination. Inspect and palpate the scalp, face, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, perineum, back and extremities while maintaining indicated spinal protection. Document wounds before they are covered when feasible and preserve forensic evidence according to policy.

Repeat the secondary survey and review final imaging because pain, sedation, intubation, distracting injury and emergency procedures hide injuries. Tertiary survey after stabilization helps find missed injury. Provide analgesia without delaying reassessment, protect pressure points, update tetanus prophylaxis, and communicate family and psychosocial needs.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify mechanism and time, catastrophic bleeding, airway and chest findings, perfusion trend, mental status, temperature, anticoagulants, pregnancy, external wounds and likely concealed compartments.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish hemorrhagic, obstructive, cardiogenic, neurogenic and distributive shock; recognize that mechanisms can coexist and that normal pressure or hemoglobin can be falsely reassuring.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Exsanguinating external hemorrhage, threatened airway, tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, tamponade and uncontrolled torso or pelvic bleeding demand immediate action.
  4. Generate solutions: Coordinate pressure, packing, tourniquet or binder; airway and chest intervention; MTP; warming and calcium; rapid imaging only when safe; and definitive operative or endovascular control.
  5. Take action: Activate the trauma pathway, document times, administer and verify warmed products, monitor access and reactions, prevent hypothermia, and communicate response continuously.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess XABCDE, bleeding, mentation, pressure and pulse trends, skin, urine, temperature, calcium, acid-base and coagulation status, respiratory findings and definitive hemostasis.

Clinical example

After a high-speed collision, a patient is pale and restless with heart rate 124/min, pressure 108/72 mm Hg, pelvic pain and an unstable lower-limb position. The initial hemoglobin is near baseline. The RN recognizes compensated hemorrhagic shock, avoids repeated pelvic manipulation, activates the trauma and MTP pathways, applies an ordered binder at the greater trochanters, obtains rapid access and emergency specimens, warms the patient and blood, and trends perfusion, calcium and coagulation. A temporary pressure rise after blood does not replace urgent pelvic hemorrhage control.

Original educational synthesis. Trauma activation, airway and chest procedures, spinal precautions, tourniquet and pelvic-binder use, imaging, blood selection and ratios, emergency release, MTP activation and termination, calcium, TXA, anticoagulant reversal, perfusion targets, surgery, embolization and transport require current patient data, authorized orders, device instructions, transfusion-service and local trauma protocols, and qualified trauma specialists. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, certification, or an official ACS or JTS product.
